edition.title: Autumn Is Here
edition.coverAlt: Journalmus No. 2, October — Autumn Is Here
edition.subtitle: Cozy rituals, green escapes, matcha stops, films, and Paris in autumn.

children.text: Hello, dear readers! Autumn has finally arrived, and Parismus is welcoming it with open arms! It’s time to get back to our good old habits: bringing out our sweaters, enjoying cozy cafés, strolling through streets covered in golden leaves and, above all, taking the time to enjoy a season that is both romantic and inspiring.
Narmin

articles.title: Autumn: Why Do We Love Our Cozy Rituals So Much?
articles.subtitle: The little habits that make the season feel like home.
articles.author: Loreane
articles.excerpt: Cinnamon rolls, pumpkin spice, cozy blankets, and familiar shows: why do we return to our autumn rituals every year?
articles.imageAlt: An autumn walkway covered in golden leaves

children.text: The leaves are turning shades of orange and gently falling beneath our feet. There’s no doubt about it—fall is here! Even when the rain rolls in, this season feels like a comforting break from our daily routine.

Beyond fleeting fads, fall traditions are now firmly rooted in our lives. Every year, it’s the same ritual: the return of cinnamon, warm cinnamon rolls, pumpkin spice lattes, cozy blankets, and evenings spent watching Gilmore Girls. But why do we love coming back to them so much?

Because we humans need a sense of stability. These cozy habits give us a feeling of security and happy nostalgia. As the cold weather approaches, rediscovering these familiar little pleasures makes us feel good and brings us together.

In terms of style, the transition happens naturally: we leave behind the bright colors of summer to embrace the warmth of brown, burgundy, or terracotta. These traditions don’t lose their appeal—they’re meant to be savored. And you—what’s the fall ritual you couldn’t live without?

articles.title: Bois de Vincennes
articles.subtitle: A leafy escape for walks, boats, gardens, and a little breathing room.
articles.author: Raquel
articles.excerpt: Welcome autumn with a walk through the gardens, lakes, and quiet paths of the Bois de Vincennes.
articles.imageAlt: A pavilion reflected in a lake at Bois de Vincennes

children.text: To properly welcome the arrival of autumn, we recommend heading to the Bois de Vincennes. This vast green space covers almost 10% of Paris’s total area. It is a true playground for walkers, sports enthusiasts, families, and anyone who loves nature!

Once reserved for royal hunting parties, this historic site has changed considerably over the years. With its botanical gardens, zoo, horse-racing track, and cultural spaces, it has become the perfect place to discover biodiversity, enjoy a wide range of activities, and take a real break from the hustle and bustle of Paris.

The Parc Floral de Paris, the capital’s largest horticultural park, can also be found here. It is a paradise for nature lovers, with beautiful themed gardens, stunning floral displays, and small art and botanical exhibitions that change with the seasons.

And let’s not forget the two artificial lakes in the Bois de Vincennes: Lac Daumesnil and Lac des Minimes. You can rent a rowboat for a charming ride on the water (available from March to November, with a deposit required). Take advantage of the many paths for a relaxing walk, a running session, or a family outing. You can also unwind in picnic areas, tucked away in peaceful corners of the park.
So grab your jacket, enjoy the autumn colors, and escape the Parisian rush for a little while!

articles.title: Pop-Up Milia Matcha
articles.subtitle: A new banana matcha joins the menu at La Samaritaine.
articles.author: Narmin
articles.excerpt: A French matcha brand brings Japanese tea traditions and playful flavors to a pop-up at La Samaritaine.
articles.imageAlt: Milia Matcha pop-up poster and banana matcha

children.text: For all matcha lovers, I highly recommend stopping by the Milia Matcha pop-up store at La Samaritaine, which will be there from October 3rd to November 1st.

Milia Matcha is a French brand specializing in Japanese matcha, founded by Andie, a French YouTuber also known as Madame Matcha. The brand officially launched in November 2023, after more than a year of research and development. Its goal is to offer 100% Japanese matcha while giving it a more modern image and creating a connection between Japanese culture and a wider audience.

The brand offers several varieties of matcha, including ceremonial matcha, as well as flavored versions such as vanilla, white chocolate, strawberry, cherry, and banana. The banana flavor became a permanent addition to the range in October.

Milia Matcha’s goal is to preserve the authentic taste of matcha while adding different flavors. At the pop-up store, visitors can choose between vanilla matcha and banana matcha, the brand’s newest flavor.

After trying it without knowing the brand beforehand, I would definitely recommend it! The banana matcha offers a surprising combination of the vegetal taste of pure matcha and a sweet, fruity banana aftertaste.
So, if you are a matcha fan and happen to be visiting La Samaritaine, don’t hesitate to stop by the Milia Matcha pop-up store!

articles.title: The Love Hypothesis
articles.subtitle: A book-to-screen rom-com, reviewed by a reader who came in with fresh eyes.
articles.author: My Linh
articles.excerpt: My Linh shares her thoughts on the screen adaptation of Ali Hazelwood’s much-loved STEM romance.
articles.imageAlt: The Love Hypothesis film poster featuring Lili Reinhart and Tom Bateman

children.text: How can I not mention the movie adaptation of the long-awaited book The Love Hypothesis by Ali Hazelwood? The movie was released on Prime Video on Wednesday, September 23rd. Being a huge rom-com fan—and having been on BookTok in 2021—I was excited to watch it.

Ali Hazelwood is known for romance books that set their characters in the world of science. Her books highlight the place of women in STEM, but also expose the unfairness they go through. Her stories hook us with lovely but unique characters who are more than likeable. The Love Hypothesis was released in 2022, and its lovely blue cover was everywhere. In 2026, after the book’s huge success, we were lucky to get an adaptation starring Lili Reinhart, the actress who played Betty in Riverdale.

Now that the context has been set, what about the movie itself? I hadn’t read the book again since its release, so I didn’t remember a thing and had a fresh pair of eyes throughout the movie. That was great because I didn’t spend the whole time comparing it with the book.

I adored it. It was funny, and the romance was well built. Yes, the movie isn’t exactly accurate, but I was nonetheless pleased. I had my eyes watering thanks to the touching friendship of Olive and Anh. My heart was pounding because of the beaming and evident chemistry between Olive and Adam. I want to see it again!
This movie is more than comforting, and you’d be missing something if you’ve read the book. It’s a good rom-com.

articles.title: Latin Quarter Walk
articles.subtitle: A Culture Team itinerary through landmarks, hidden lanes, and layers of Parisian history.
articles.author: Narmin
articles.excerpt: Follow the Culture Team from the Odéon Theatre and the Sorbonne to the Panthéon on a walk through the Latin Quarter.
articles.imageAlt: The Panthéon in the Latin Quarter

children.text: For our first cultural tour, our Culture Department coordinators, Maya and Louanne, had prepared an exciting itinerary to explore the Latin Quarter, taking us through iconic landmarks, hidden corners, and some of the most fascinating chapters of Parisian history.

Our tour began at the Odéon Theatre, built in the 18th century under Louis XVI. This first stop immediately set the tone: the Latin Quarter has always been a place where culture plays a central role. We then stopped at Place de la Sorbonne and the famous university, whose origins date back to the Middle Ages and which remains one of the district’s most iconic landmarks.

We continued to the Musée de Cluny, a true summary of the history of the Latin Quarter. The museum notably houses the remains of the ancient Roman baths of Lutetia, offering a glimpse into Paris’s Roman past.

Our itinerary then took us along the banks of the Seine, before leading us through some of the district’s most characteristic streets. We passed through Rue de la Huchette and Rue du Chat-qui-Pêche, considered the narrowest street in Paris. These small passages are part of what gives the Latin Quarter its unique charm.

The tour continued with a stop at Shakespeare and Company, the famous English-language bookshop opposite Notre-Dame, followed by a walk through Rue Galande, Rue Dante, and Rue du Fouarre, where traces of medieval Paris and its university history can still be found. We then reached Quai de la Tournelle, famous for its traditional booksellers, before continuing to the Institut du Monde Arabe, opened in 1987.

We then changed eras once again with the Jardin des Plantes, established in 1635 as a royal garden for doctors and apothecaries. A few streets further on, the Arènes de Lutèce brought us back to Roman times, reminding us that the Latin Quarter lies at the heart of ancient Lutetia.

Finally, we discovered the remains of Philippe Auguste’s city walls, one of the last traces of medieval Paris, before ending our tour at the Bibliothèque Sainte-Geneviève and the Panthéon. Between knowledge, history, and national heritage, these two monuments provided the perfect ending to our journey.

Throughout this itinerary, we discovered much more than just another Parisian neighborhood: a true concentration of history, culture, and heritage, where almost every street seems to tell the story of a different era.

articles.title: That’s So French
articles.subtitle: Four little cultural facts for your next café conversation.
articles.author: Mariem
articles.excerpt: Long café breaks, endless cheese debates, a once-temporary tower, and a baguette on UNESCO’s heritage list.

children.text: In France, ordering a coffee can sometimes take two minutes, but sitting on a café terrace with that same coffee can last two hours. That’s so French.
In France, there are more than 1,000 varieties of cheese, and you can easily end up debating which one is the best. That’s so French.
The Eiffel Tower was only meant to be temporary. It was supposed to be dismantled after 20 years, but instead it became an icon of the country. That’s so French.
The baguette is so important to the French that it has been added to UNESCO’s Intangible Cultural Heritage list. That’s so French.
